name: Jonah

objectives.text: Identify Jonah as the prophet God sent to Nineveh who was swallowed by a great fish
Name Nineveh as the great city God sent Jonah to and Tarshish as the place he tried to flee to
Retell in order the main events of Jonah's flight, rescue, preaching, and complaint
Describe how God directed the storm, the fish, the plant, and the worm to show that he rules over all creation
Explain from Jonah's flight that no one can escape God's presence
Describe how the pagan sailors came to fear and worship the LORD during the storm
Describe how the king and people of Nineveh responded to Jonah's message and how God spared the city
Explain why Jonah was angry at God's mercy using his own words in chapter 4
Compare God's compassion for Nineveh with Jonah's concern for the plant
Connect Jonah's description of God in Jonah 4:2 to the LORD's self-revelation to Moses
Explain how God's concern for Nineveh relates to Jesus' command to love one's enemies
Locate Jonah's ministry in the reign of Jeroboam II and describe Assyria's place as Israel's rising enemy
Analyze Jonah's prayer from the fish as a psalm of thanksgiving, noting its echoes of the Psalms and its climax that salvation belongs to the LORD
Interpret the sign of Jonah as Jesus applied it to his death, resurrection, and the judgment of his generation
Analyze how Jonah's conduct reflects Israel's calling to bless the nations and its failure to fulfill that calling
Analyze the irony in the narrative, including the prophet's repeated going down and the quick obedience of pagans contrasted with the prophet's resistance
Analyze how God's relenting from judgment on Nineveh fits with the Reformed confession of God's unchanging nature and decree
Use biblical and historical evidence of Assyrian cruelty to explain Jonah's reluctance to preach to Nineveh
Compare Jonah's mission to Nineveh with Peter's mission from Joppa to the Gentile Cornelius
Evaluate the purpose of the book ending with God's unanswered question to Jonah
Evaluate historical and parable readings of the book and articulate the Reformed tradition's case for its historicity
Construct an account tracing God's purpose to save people from the nations from Abraham through Jonah to the Great Commission

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (identifying Jonah and Nineveh, retelling, Jonah's anger, comparing mercy and anger, the prayer, the sign of Jonah, Israel's calling, irony, Assyrian background, the ending, historicity, God's mission). Merged the separate retell and summarize objectives into one. Recast 'you can't run away from God' and 'God cares for our enemies' as explanations grounded in texts rather than personal application. Dropped the vague 'God loves people everywhere' recall. Added God's providence over creation, the sailors' response, Nineveh's repentance, the Exodus 34 echo, the historical setting under Jeroboam II, God's relenting and immutability, and the Jonah and Peter comparison. Added verse-level scripture and confessional anchors where the doctrine is stated.
